passages.happening:
“When the day of Pentecost came, they were all together in one place” (verse 1).

Suddenly a sound like a mighty rushing wind comes from heaven and fills the house. They see “tongues like flames of fire” that separate and rest on each of them (verse 3). “And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit enabled them” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Pentecost is Greek for ‘fiftieth’. It was the Jewish Feast of Weeks, held fifty days after Passover, when the first wheat harvest was offered to God. It was one of the three feasts when the law called every Israelite man to come to Jerusalem, so the city was crowded with pilgrims. Jesus had died at Passover. Seven weeks later, the Spirit comes.

Later Jewish tradition also tied the Feast of Weeks to the day God gave the law at Mount Sinai. The rabbis say this clearly, and an older book called Jubilees, from the second century BC, links the feast with God's covenant. How widely Jews in Peter's day made the link is debated. If they did, the Spirit's coming on that day would have carried extra meaning: the law was given at Sinai, and now the Spirit is given in Jerusalem.

Wind and fire were old signs that God himself had come near. In Hebrew and in Greek the same word can mean wind, breath or spirit. And John the Baptist had promised that Jesus would baptize “with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (Luke 3:16).

Notice the word ‘each’. The fire rests on each of them, and all of them are filled. The Spirit is not given only to the apostles, but to the whole gathering, about a hundred and twenty men and women (1:14-15).
passages.ot:
The feast itself comes from the Law: “You shall count off fifty days until the day after the seventh Sabbath, and then present an offering of new grain to the LORD” (Leviticus 23:16; compare Deuteronomy 16:9-10).

Fire and the sound of God's coming recall Sinai: “Mount Sinai was completely enveloped in smoke, because the LORD had descended on it in fire” (Exodus 19:18). And many readers think of Babel, where God “confused the language of the whole world” and scattered the nations (Genesis 11:9). At Pentecost the languages are not taken away, but people of many languages hear one message.

Long before, Moses had said, “I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets and that the LORD would place His Spirit on them” (Numbers 11:29). Here that wish begins to come true.
passages.hard:
What were these ‘tongues’, and does God give the gift today?

In this chapter the tongues are known human languages. Luke says so plainly: the crowd from many lands “heard them speaking his own language” (verse 6), and they name the places they come from. Some readers have asked whether the miracle was in the speaking or in the hearing. Luke tells of both: the believers “began to speak in other tongues” and each listener heard his own language.

Elsewhere the New Testament speaks of a gift of tongues that no one understands without an interpreter (1 Corinthians 14:2, 27-28). Christians differ on whether this is the same gift as Acts 2 or a different one.

Christians also differ on whether the gift continues today. These views are held by faithful believers, and these notes do not choose between them.

Pentecostal Christians, a movement that grew from revivals in the United States in the early 1900s (at Topeka, Kansas, in 1901 and at Azusa Street in Los Angeles in 1906), teach that believers may receive a baptism in the Spirit after they come to faith, for power to witness. Classical Pentecostal churches, such as the Assemblies of God, teach that speaking in tongues is the first outward sign of that baptism.

Charismatic Christians, found in many churches, Catholic and Protestant, welcome tongues and the other gifts today, but most do not teach that every Spirit-filled believer must speak in tongues.

Continuationists hold that all the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12, tongues among them, continue in the church, while also holding that every believer receives the Spirit when he or she comes to faith, and that not everyone will speak in tongues; Paul asks, “Do all speak in tongues?” (1 Corinthians 12:30), and the expected answer is no.

Cessationists hold that tongues and other sign gifts belonged to the time of the apostles, to confirm their message while the New Testament was being given, and then ceased. B. B. Warfield argued this in Counterfeit Miracles (1918). Most cessationists still believe God answers prayer and can do wonders today; they deny only that these gifts are given as before.

All of them agree on what matters most in this chapter: the Spirit is the gift of the risen Jesus to his whole church, and he came so that people of every language might hear of God's mighty works.
passages.asks: The Spirit did not come to give the believers a private thrill. He came, and at once they were speaking to others. Ask what the Spirit's presence in a church is for, and whether your own faith is turned outward toward people who have not yet heard.

passages.happening:
In Jerusalem there were “God-fearing Jews from every nation under heaven” (verse 5). When they hear the sound, a crowd gathers, amazed, “because each one heard them speaking his own language” (verse 6). “Are not all these men who are speaking Galileans?” they ask (verse 7).

Luke lists where they came from: Parthians, Medes and Elamites; people from Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and Libya near Cyrene; visitors from Rome, “both Jews and converts to Judaism”; Cretans and Arabs (verses 9-11). They hear them “declaring the wonders of God in our own tongues”.

Some are amazed and ask, “What does this mean?” Others mock: “They are drunk on new wine” (verses 12-13).
passages.hearers:
These listeners were Jews, and Gentiles who had become Jews (converts, sometimes called proselytes). Jews had lived scattered across the world for centuries, since the exile to Babylon; this scattering is called the Diaspora. Some had come to Jerusalem for the feast, and others had settled there to live near the temple.

The list sweeps roughly from east to west: from Parthia and Media, beyond the Roman Empire's eastern edge, through Mesopotamia and what is now Turkey, to Egypt and North Africa, and on to Rome. It is a picture of the whole Jewish world, gathered in one street.

Galileans spoke with an accent the city people noticed; on the night of Jesus' arrest, a bystander told Peter, “your accent gives you away” (Matthew 26:73). So the surprise is real. Country men from the north are speaking the languages of distant lands.

Every miracle in Acts gets two responses. Some are amazed and ask questions. Some mock. Luke does not hide the mockers.
passages.ot:
The prophets had promised that God would gather his scattered people from every land. Isaiah heard God say, “I will bring your offspring from the east and gather you from the west” (Isaiah 43:5). That gathering begins here, at a feast, in Jerusalem.

The list of nations also reminds many readers of the list of the world's peoples in Genesis 10, which comes just before Babel in Genesis 11. The nations scattered there are, in picture, gathered here.
passages.asks: God's first act after sending the Spirit was to speak to people in their own mother tongue. Ask what that says about how God regards the languages, homes and cultures of the people he calls. And ask which kind of hearer you tend to be when God does something unexpected: the one who asks what it means, or the one who mocks.

passages.happening:
Peter stands up with the Eleven and speaks to the crowd. “These men are not drunk, as you suppose. It is only the third hour of the day” (verse 15). The third hour was about nine in the morning.

“No, this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel” (verse 16). Then he quotes Joel: God will pour out his Spirit on all people; sons and daughters will prophesy, young men will see visions and old men dream dreams; even on servants, men and women, God will pour out his Spirit. There will be wonders in the heavens and signs on the earth before the great Day of the Lord. “And everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
This is the first Christian sermon. It begins where the hearers are, with what they have just seen and heard, and then it opens Scripture.

The fisherman who seven weeks earlier had denied knowing Jesus to a servant girl now stands up before thousands. That change is part of Luke's point. The Spirit gives courage.

Joel's words were striking for their reach. The Spirit in Israel's story had mostly come on a few: prophets, judges, kings. Now God promises the Spirit to ‘all people’: young and old, sons and daughters, even slaves. No one is too low or too young or too female to be filled. In the first century that was a startling claim.

Peter makes one change at the start. Joel says “afterward”; Peter says “In the last days”. He is telling the crowd what time it is. The last days, the time the prophets looked forward to, have begun.
passages.ot:
The words come from Joel 2:28-32. In Joel they follow a terrible plague of locusts and a call to return to God. Then comes the promise: “And afterward, I will pour out My Spirit on all people” (Joel 2:28).

Peter's quotation has small differences from Joel's wording, and it stops part way through Joel 2:32 at “everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved”. In Joel ‘the LORD’ is the name of Israel's God. By the end of the sermon Peter will say that God has made Jesus ‘Lord’ (verse 36). Many readers see that as the key to the whole speech: to call on the name of the Lord is now to call on Jesus.
passages.asks: Peter answered mockery with Scripture, not with anger. Ask how you respond when what you believe is laughed at. And notice who Joel says receives the Spirit: sons and daughters, old and young, servants. Ask whether your church expects God to speak through the people it tends to overlook.

passages.t: Jesus of Nazareth, killed and raised
passages.happening:
“Men of Israel, listen to this message” (verse 22). Peter tells them about Jesus of Nazareth, a man God showed to them by miracles, wonders and signs, “as you yourselves know”.

“He was delivered up by God’s set plan and foreknowledge, and you, by the hands of the lawless, put Him to death by nailing Him to the cross” (verse 23). “But God raised Him from the dead, releasing Him from the agony of death, because it was impossible for Him to be held in its clutches” (verse 24).

Then he quotes David: “I saw the Lord always before me”, and “You will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay” (verses 25-27).
passages.hearers:
Peter speaks to people who had been in Jerusalem seven weeks earlier, at Passover. Some of them may have been in the crowd before Pilate. He appeals to what they know: Jesus' deeds were done ‘among you’.

He holds two truths together in one sentence. Jesus died by ‘God's set plan’, and yet the people who brought it about are responsible. Scripture does this often: God's purpose stands, and human choices are still real choices.

‘The lawless’ means people outside God's law, the Gentiles, here the Roman soldiers who did the crucifying. So Peter names both: the Jerusalem leaders and crowd who handed Jesus over, and the Romans who nailed him up.

Hades is the Greek word for the place of the dead, the same as Sheol in the Hebrew Bible. Peter's claim is that death could not keep Jesus. Luke's word for ‘agony’ is the word for the pains of childbirth, and some readers hear in it a picture of death in labour, unable to hold back the life it held.
passages.ot:
Peter quotes Psalm 16:8-11, a psalm of David: “For You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay” (Psalm 16:10). In the psalm David trusts that God will not hand him over to death. Peter will argue in the next verses that these words go further than David's own life, because David did die and stay buried.

‘Delivered up’ by God's plan echoes Isaiah's servant: “Yet it was the LORD’s will to crush Him and to cause Him to suffer” (Isaiah 53:10).
passages.hard:
Peter says ‘you’ put Jesus to death (verse 23), and later ‘whom you crucified’ (verse 36). How should those words be read?

First, see who is speaking, and to whom. Peter is a Jew, speaking to his own people, in their own city, weeks after the event, about something done there. He includes the Romans (‘the lawless’) in the same sentence. He says Jesus was delivered up by God's own plan. In his next sermon he adds, “I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your leaders” (3:17). And he does not condemn them; he offers them forgiveness, and three thousand of the hearers believe and are baptized. This is a prophet's call to his own nation to turn, like the calls of Jeremiah and the other prophets, not a verdict on a people.

For centuries many Christians called the Jewish people ‘Christ-killers’ and used scenes like this to justify contempt, expulsions, and violence against Jews. That reading is false, and Christians must reject it plainly. This site rejects it. Jesus himself, his disciples, and the crowds who welcomed him were Jews; so were Peter and the three thousand who believed that day. A Roman governor gave the order, and Roman soldiers carried it out. In 1965 the Catholic Church's Second Vatican Council said that what happened in the passion ‘cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today’. Most churches teach the same. The New Testament places all people inside the guilt: in Acts the first Christians pray that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel all stood together against Jesus (Acts 4:27).
passages.asks: Peter told his hearers the hardest thing they could hear, that they had helped kill the Messiah, and he told it so that they could be forgiven. Ask whether you have ever let the cross of Jesus show you your own part in the world's wrong, and not only someone else's. The message of Acts is that no one is beyond the reach of that forgiveness.

passages.happening:
“Brothers, I can tell you with confidence that the patriarch David died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day” (verse 29). But David was a prophet. God had promised him on oath to set one of his descendants on his throne. So David “spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that He was not abandoned to Hades, nor did His body see decay” (verse 31).

“God has raised this Jesus to life, to which we are all witnesses” (verse 32). Exalted to God's right hand, he has received the promised Spirit from the Father “and has poured out what you now see and hear” (verse 33).

David did not go up to heaven, Peter says, yet he said, “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet’” (verses 34-35). “Therefore let all Israel know with certainty that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ” (verse 36).
passages.hearers:
Peter argues the way Jewish teachers argued: from Scripture, step by step. David's tomb was a known place in Jerusalem. Everyone could see that David's body had stayed in the grave. So when David wrote of one whom God would not let ‘see decay’, he must have been looking ahead to his greater descendant, the Christ. And unlike David's tomb, Jesus' tomb was empty, and Peter and the others had seen him alive.

‘Christ’ is the Greek form of ‘Messiah’: the anointed king God had promised from David's line. ‘Lord’ is the word the Greek Bible used for God's own name. Peter gives Jesus both.

The ‘right hand’ was the place of honour and power beside a king. To say Jesus sits at God's right hand is to say he rules with God. And the gift the crowd has just seen and heard is the proof: the risen Jesus has poured out the Spirit.
passages.ot:
Two passages carry the argument. God's promise to David: “I will raise up your descendant after you” and “I will establish his kingdom” (2 Samuel 7:12), and “I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (2 Samuel 7:13). And Psalm 110:1, a verse the New Testament quotes and echoes many times: “The LORD said to my Lord: ‘Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet’”.

Jesus himself had asked the teachers of his day how David could call his own descendant ‘Lord’ (Luke 20:41-44). Peter now gives the answer.
passages.hard: ‘Whom you crucified’ (verse 36) is the sharpest line of the sermon. The note on verses 22-28 above sets out how it must be read: a Jew calling his own people to turn, with God's purpose named and forgiveness offered, and never a charge against the Jewish people, which this site rejects. The very next verse shows the hearers ‘cut to the heart’, asking what to do, and Peter answers them with a promise.
passages.asks: The sermon ends not with advice but with a claim about who Jesus is: Lord and Christ. Ask what it would mean in your own life to treat Jesus not only as a helper or a teacher, but as Lord, the one at God's right hand. Everything else Peter says next depends on that.

passages.happening:
“When the people heard this, they were cut to the heart and asked Peter and the other apostles, ‘Brothers, what shall we do?’” (verse 37).

“Peter replied, ‘Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit’” (verse 38). The promise, he says, “belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off” (verse 39), to all whom the Lord will call.

He urges them, “Be saved from this corrupt generation” (verse 40). “Those who embraced his message were baptized, and about three thousand were added to the believers that day” (verse 41).
passages.hearers:
‘Repent’ means to turn around: a change of mind that becomes a change of life. For these hearers it meant changing their minds about Jesus, from a man rightly put to death to the Lord and Christ.

Baptism was a washing with water. Jews knew washings for purity, and John the Baptist had baptized people who repented. Baptism ‘in the name of Jesus Christ’ marked a person as belonging to Jesus.

‘All who are far off’ may mean Jews scattered far from Jerusalem, or it may already reach to the Gentiles. Paul later uses the same words of Gentiles: “you who once were far away have been brought near” (Ephesians 2:13).

Three thousand in a day is a great number. Luke does not say where or how they were baptized.
passages.ot:
‘All who are far off’ echoes Isaiah: “Peace, peace to those far and near,” says the LORD, “and I will heal them” (Isaiah 57:19). And ‘all whom the Lord our God will call’ echoes the end of the same verse of Joel that Peter has just quoted: deliverance will be “among the remnant called by the LORD” (Joel 2:32).

The promise ‘to you and your children’ recalls God's covenant with Abraham, made with him and his offspring after him (Genesis 17:7).
passages.hard:
What does verse 38 teach about baptism and forgiveness, and what does ‘you and your children’ mean? Churches read it differently, and the differences are old and sincerely held. These notes set out the main readings in the words their holders would use, and do not choose between them.

Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold that baptism is a sacrament in which God truly forgives sins and gives new birth by the Spirit. The Catechism of the Catholic Church says, citing this verse, that by baptism all sins are forgiven (paragraph 1263). They baptize infants, and they read ‘you and your children’ as including them.

Lutherans hold that baptism is God's own work, not ours. Luther's Small Catechism teaches that baptism gives forgiveness of sins, rescue from death and the devil, and eternal salvation to all who believe God's promise. They also baptize infants.

Presbyterian and Reformed churches hold that baptism is a sign and seal of God's covenant promises, joined to the grace it signifies but not the cause of it; forgiveness is received by faith. The Westminster Confession (chapter 28) lists this passage among its proofs for baptizing the infants of believers. They read ‘you and your children’ as the covenant promise to believers' families, as God's promise to Abraham included his children.

Baptists, and many other evangelicals, hold that forgiveness comes through repentance and faith, and that baptism is the believer's public sign of that turning, commanded by Christ and following it. They baptize only those old enough to confess faith themselves. They read ‘you and your children’ as the promise reaching each generation, and they note that the verse goes on, ‘to all whom the Lord our God will call’, and that verse 41 says those who ‘embraced his message’ were baptized.

Churches of Christ, and others in the movement that grew from the work of Barton Stone and Alexander Campbell, read verse 38 plainly as teaching that a believer's baptism by immersion is the moment at which God forgives sins, and they hold that it should not be left out.

Part of the debate is about grammar. ‘Repent’ is plural, addressed to all; ‘be baptized’ is singular, ‘each of you’; and ‘for’ can mean ‘in order to’ or ‘with a view to’. Some tie the forgiveness chiefly to repentance; others answer that the two commands are joined and belong together.

What all these churches share is larger than what divides them. Repentance, faith and baptism belong together in the New Testament. Forgiveness is God's gift through Jesus Christ. And the Spirit is promised to all who belong to him. These are questions on which faithful churches differ while confessing one Lord.
passages.asks: The crowd's question is the right one: ‘What shall we do?’ Peter's answer is not ‘try harder’, but turn, be washed, and receive a gift. Ask whether you have ever answered the gospel for yourself, not only heard it. And whatever your church's view of baptism, ask what it would mean to live as someone who belongs to Jesus by name.

passages.t: The life of the first believers
passages.happening:
“They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer” (verse 42). Awe comes over everyone, and the apostles do many wonders and signs.

“All the believers were together and had everything in common. Selling their possessions and goods, they shared with anyone who was in need” (verses 44-45). Every day they meet in the temple courts and break bread in their homes, “sharing their meals with gladness and sincerity of heart” (verse 46). They praise God and enjoy the favour of all the people. “And the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved” (verse 47).
passages.hearers:
This is the first of Luke's short pictures of the church's life. Four things mark it: teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer.

‘The apostles' teaching’ was what Jesus had taught them and what they had seen. ‘Fellowship’ translates koinōnia, a sharing in common: in a life, in a meal, in goods. ‘The breaking of bread’ was a shared meal, and many readers think it included the Lord's Supper, which Jesus had given at a meal on the night before he died; others think Luke means ordinary meals here. ‘Prayer’ in Greek has ‘the’ before it, ‘the prayers’, and some think that means the set Jewish times of prayer, which the believers still kept (3:1).

These believers were still Jews in their whole way of life. They prayed in the temple. They ate in homes. Nothing yet separated them from their neighbours except that they believed Jesus was the Messiah, and they were well thought of by ‘all the people’.
passages.ot:
The Law had pictured a people in which no one lacked: “There will be no poor among you, however, because the LORD will surely bless you in the land” (Deuteronomy 15:4). Luke says almost the same about the church two chapters later: “There were no needy ones among them” (4:34). Many readers think Luke means his reader to see the old promise beginning to come true.

Gladness at shared meals before God is part of the Law's picture of the feasts too: “you shall rejoice before the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 16:11).
passages.hard:
‘Everything in common’ (verse 44). What did the first believers do, and is it a pattern?

The text says they sold possessions and goods and shared with anyone in need. It also shows they still had homes, where they broke bread (verse 46). Chapter 4 says the same in other words: people sold land and houses when there was need (4:34-35). And chapter 5 makes clear that giving was free, not forced. Peter tells Ananias that his land was his own before it was sold, and the money was his to use after (5:4).

So this was not a law, and it was not a plan run by any government. It was the free giving of people who had been given so much that they no longer held their things tightly, in one city, at one time.

This passage has often been claimed for modern economic and political programs, from more than one side. These notes make no such application of any kind, left or right. Luke describes a church, not a state. What the passage plainly asks of Christians is that no believer they know should go in need while others have more than enough, and churches have answered that call in many different ways.
passages.asks: The first church was known for four things, and none of them was a building or a program. Ask how much of your week is given to learning the faith, to real sharing with other believers, to the Lord's table and to prayer. And ask whether anyone in your circle of believers is going without while you have plenty.
